title: Warnings to Five Neighboring Nations
overview: Jeremiah announces coming disaster on Ammon, Edom, Damascus, the desert peoples of Kedar and Hazor, and Elam, while promising that some of them will one day be restored.

parts.label: Ammon loses its land (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: After Assyria deported the Israelite tribe of Gad from its land east of the Jordan, neighboring Ammon moved into its towns, and now Ammon's chief god, whose name means 'king', will be carried off with his priests. Ammon trusted its fertile valleys and wealth to keep it safe, yet it will be driven out, though verse 6 promises its fortunes will one day be restored.

parts.label: Edom stripped bare (vv. 7-13)
parts.note: Edom, traced back to Esau, Jacob's brother, was famous for its wise men in Teman, and while grape pickers and even thieves leave something behind, its invaders will leave nothing. The 'cup' stands for God's judgment: if others who seemed not to deserve it must drink it (some interpreters think Judah is meant, though the text does not say), Edom will not escape.

parts.label: Pride brought down (vv. 14-22)
parts.note: Edom lived among high cliffs and rock dwellings and felt as safe as an eagle's nest, but its pride fooled it. Much of this wording echoes the short book of Obadiah, and the lion and shepherd images picture an attacker no Edomite leader can stand against.

parts.label: Damascus in panic (vv. 23-27)
parts.note: Damascus, in what is now Syria, and its northern neighbors Hamath and Arpad hear bad news and are seized with fear. Verse 25 is puzzling and is often read as a citizen grieving a beloved city, and Ben-Hadad was the name of earlier Damascus kings who fought Israel.

parts.label: Kedar and Hazor raided (vv. 28-33)
parts.note: Kedar and Hazor here seem to be Arabian desert peoples living in tents with camels and herds, who felt safe without walls because they were so remote. Babylon did campaign against Arab tribes in this period, and 'terror on every side' is a phrase Jeremiah uses often.

parts.label: Elam scattered, then restored (vv. 34-39)
parts.note: Elam lay east of Babylon in what is now southwest Iran and was known for its archers, so breaking its bow means breaking its main strength, and the four winds picture its people scattered everywhere. The chapter ends with a promise of restoration, which Christians have read alongside the Elamites in the crowd hearing the apostles in Acts 2.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether these oracles were fully fulfilled in ancient history or still point to future events, especially the promises of restoration.
think: When a person or a nation feels untouchable because of wealth, walls or distance, what do you think usually ends that feeling?
